catalog_locator: Ch. 3, sec. 3.4 'The Kora system of tone melodies' p. 97 (lexical tone; register tones); sec. 3.4.1 'The citation melodies of Kora' pp. 97-98 (citation-form do…
catalog_quote: Like all other Khoisan languages, Kora makes use of lexical tone. [...] All of these studies treat the tones as register tones (rather than contour tones), where each tone is carried individually by a vowel or a nasal. [...] The tone melodies of the Khoekhoe languages typically have a basic (or ‘citation’) form, which is to say, the melody that is used when a word is spoken in isolation or at the beginning of a sentence. These melodies change systematically in certain syntactic contexts [...] (Maingard established through correspondence with Lloyd’s niece Dorothea Bleek that in her aunt’s system, the acute accent was usually intended to indicate stress.) [...] What we hear in Ouma Jacoba’s speech is nevertheless a set of four clearly distinct tone melodies – just as expected, where two are level [H-H] and [L-L], one rises [L-H] and one falls [H-L].
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kora is described purely as a lexical-tone language: each root carries one of four citation tone melodies (HH, LL, LH, HL) over two morae, with systematic alternant melodies in compounds and phrase-finally. The modern description gives no rule for, and makes no claim about, word stress; the only references to stress in the Korana literature opened are historiographic (Lucy Lloyd's 1870s acute accents reportedly marked stress, which Maingard 1932 found 'very complicated' and left unanalysed).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. du Plessis notes ideophones may show 'unusual stress patterns' (ch. 4 p. 174), a generic remark. Maingard 1932: 158-159 says of one proper name (gei !hareip) that 'the tone and stress are on the last syllable' -- an isolated observation, not a rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone melodies are given for citation forms (isolation / sentence-initial), with sandhi alternants in compounds and phrase-final position; no word-stress domain is defined anywhere.
new_statements.identity_note: du Plessis 2018's own recordings are of two last speakers from the Bloemhof Korana (Ouma Jacoba Maclear), while Beach 1938's tonal data (reprinted in her Table 3.5) are from a Kimberley Korana speaker; Killian 2009 uses the cover term Khoemana for Korana + Griqua (Glottolog kora1292 covers both; Griqua/Xiri has its own ISO xii). All refer to the same language, kora1292.

sources.note: Nothing on word stress. States Kora 'makes use of lexical tone' (register tones, two morae per root) with four citation melodies (HH, LL, LH, HL) plus sandhi/compound alternants; the only mention of stress is historiographic (p. 98: Lucy Lloyd's acute accents were 'usually intended to indicate stress' per D. Bleek via Maingard).

sources.citation: Maingard, L. F. 1932. Studies in Korana history, customs and language. Bantu Studies 6: 103-162 (sec. VI Language, pp. 148-153; (c) Tones p. 150).
sources.note: Phonology section covers vowels, consonants, clicks and tones ('the Bloemhof speech uses tones... One incidental remark (p. 158-159) that in the name gei !hareip 'the tone and stress are on the last syllable' -- a single word, not a rule.
